en: This walnut I have brought
I give to Akbermet and Seytek
As a gift held in sacred trust.
This Kertulpar standing here
Was born by supernatural power and has journeyed here;
It is destined for him to mount in war.
For the fierce hero Kenen
This was written upon his brow.
A three-year-old this year, a two-year-old last,
Every mark of a tulpar is complete.
Born by magic and raised in the desert,
Raised upon a dark and rugged ridge,
Raised in a place where neither human, beast,
Nor any living creature ever looked,
It raced the wild asses stride for stride.
With the steeds of bygone mighty Kalmyks—
Kongurbai’s Algara,
Orok Kyr’s Kylkara,
Börüköz’s Kertelki,
And Jaidaksur ridden by the commander—
The warhorses of the giant warriors,
It was born of the same stock
And raced beside the wild asses.
It drank from the Kaimana,
And grazed upon sacred herbs.
The copper hag among horse judges
Who tended it on Mount Barbar
Declared, “This is a true tulpar.”
“This mad creature is like a whirlwind;
Might it take flight?” she said,
And that peerless judge approved it.
Its hoof does not sink into water;
My far-seeing ancestor Körögöch
And my wise father praised it.
When it gathers itself, its stride stretches wide;
By God’s decree and fortune’s aid,
It has been bestowed upon hero Kenen.
Kertulpar will grow into a mighty steed;
Whoever asks to take it will be a stranger.
Broad-lunged and copper-sinewed,
With a wild ass’s haunches and lean feet,
This is the very image of a perfect tulpar.
Roman-nosed and high-crested,
It will not flinch when mounted for battle;
Broad-chested and low-maned,
It will not falter before an open foe.
If, after hardship, its rider cries, “Go!”
No living soul can flee and escape it.
Fail to tell this plainly, and shame will follow;
For Kenen, who is yet to be born,
You must give it, Joltay, as a sacred trust!
The man who had spoken thus
Now vanished from sight.
Leading the entrusted Kertulpar
Unsaddled beside him, he pressed onward,
Praying to the Creator.
That supremely wise sage,
Who had seen distant lands from afar,
Your venerable forefather Joltay
Along a separate, low-lying road
Now turned back—behold him.
Joltay journeyed on and came;
The sheep rustled in their fold,
Light spilled over the earth,
And the world appeared radiant.
Dawn broke as though the earth had split,
Sunlight touched mountain after mountain,
The nightingale sang in the forest,
And the drifting haze dispersed.
Marked waters, stones, and everything else
Stood as plain as five spread fingers.
Just as the world appeared so,
To the palace with its stout gate,
To the fortress with its portals,
Valiant Joltay came.
Without uttering a single word,
He hastened in at a run;
From atop his mountain-like gray horse,
Joltay rushed onward without pause,
With the dignity of a princely pasha,
He entered the palace—
Your uncle Akjoltay.
With uncommon foresight he made his plan;
Turning toward his right,
Without letting anyone know,
Without alerting a single soul,
He leaned aside,
Filled out his robe,
Slipped his hand into his pouch,
And drew out a fist-sized object.
Disregard it and shame will follow:
“My steadfast child Akbermet,
This pale walnut, large as a fist,
The holy wanderer Khizr
Has entrusted to you.
Eat it, my little one;
Your grime-covered heart will open,
And your frenzy will subside.
My child Bermet, heed me:
I have become your healer.
May you be mother of the nation
That bears a lionhearted champion.
Accept your trust, my child,
Purest among women in flowing skirts,
Foremost among women in white kerchiefs.
Eat it, and it will quench your thirst;
Give your great blessing, my child.
Say, ‘My uncle has left me an inheritance’;
Regard this service of mine, my child.”
When Akbermet heard this,
She walked forward glowing,
Shining like the risen moon,
Blooming like a parrot’s plumage,
Revealing the graces of ninety tribes,
That hapless fairy princess.
Her sacred virtue became manifest.
Before dear uncle Joltay
She sprang like a bow and bowed,
With prayer beads hung about her neck,
And pleaded beyond all measure:
“My uncle Joltay, peerless khan,
You who join what has been severed,
Who gathered all these people,
Who mended what was broken,
My undeserved good fortune,
My sheltering presence, my destiny.”
Speaking thus, Akbermet
Bent her neck and trembled,
Imploring her uncle,
Her whole being melting,
Her flesh and nails reaching out.
When he had told her the true tidings,
Her tiny soul cried out,
And she wept in sincere supplication.
As soon as she ate that walnut,
Her frenzy subsided,
Her mind cleared in contemplation,
The grime upon her heart fell away,
And strength entered and filled her.
Overcome with joy, she trembled:
“I have repented ninetyfold,” she said,
Bowing her dear head down to the earth.
“Uncle Joltay, may you live long;
I have always looked to you for shelter.
I will not assail you with harsh words;
You are the spiritual guide I humbly implore,
And I will never cease to hope in you.”
Thus spoke Akbermet.
As she stood there in this wondrous state,
And finished speaking
To her uncle Joltay, the gray wolf,
Seytek readied himself like a hawk;
Into the lion Seytek’s mind
An inspiration came from the unseen.
In a dream, his forefather hero Manas
Revealed an auspicious vision.
It was his forefather Manas himself,
The radiant one supporting and sustaining him,
Who had come to visit him then.
He placed a sword in my hand,
And spoke at length of its thousand-fold lineage:
“Take heed, my child,” he said,
“You are my joy, you are my root,
You are the heir who carries on my legacy.
In this worthless, deceitful world,
Do not be vainly tempted, my child;
Do not chill the people’s hearts.
Do not lord it over those beneath you,
And never treat the poor, the orphaned, the wretched
With contempt, my son!
My forefather Manas said these words:
‘Here is Zulpuqor before you;
I give it to you, my son—take it.
A son as keen as Zulpuqor
Will come into your arms.
When you take this sword in hand,
Whoever faces you will swiftly perish;
When you strike straight, it will blaze like fire.
The land you charge against will be laid waste,
And its people will despair of life.
Of every hostile enemy,
It will level the innermost fortress.
When you draw it, its edge will glow red.
I give it to you, my son—take it,
Bind it firmly to your arm,
Do not loose it toward whatever lies before you,
But guard it securely and wait.
Solitude is suffering,’ he said.
‘All the cares that weigh upon your life—
May you sweep every one of them away.
God willing, a son will be born;
Name him Kenen.
If that son survives,
My child, he himself will inherit from you.
That son will be of the ancient line,
A lofty plane tree, a proud banner to his foes,
With eyes like deep and boundless springs,
The very image of a gray-maned wolf.
Prize the sword and place it in its sheath;
Then go against the enemy
Who flaunts his might and boasts,
Spill his blood and turn him back.
If a hostile foe advances upon you,
Break his back when you meet,
Still his heart when you clash,
Spilling blood and scorching the earth.
Wage the struggle fiercely!’
Thus spoke my grandfather,
And when he spread his hands and said, ‘Amen,’
There were eighty men behind him
And eight men before him.
When my forefather gave his blessing,
They all gave their blessing too.
Their white beards gleamed like pale silk,
Their shining teeth were like copper,
Their blue eyes were round as great bowls,
Their splendor seemed enough to swallow one’s soul.
All were gathered there together:
Almambet and Chubak among them,
And the elders Koshoy and Bakai.
With a great roar they raised their hands—
All the companions
Of my lion-hearted father Manas.
Having received the heroes’ blessing,
I awoke with a start from sleep.
It was a dream seen by grace,
With my forefather Manas at their head;
It was a day when blessings were bestowed,
A wondrous and auspicious thing,
A dream from which I woke in alarm.
What might this dream of mine portend?
Let uncle Akjoltoy interpret it now!”
Then his uncle Joltay
Readied himself like a hawk,
And prayed to the spirit
Of the hero who had passed into the next world:
“May your dream, my child, come true.
If your forefather gave you Zulpuqor,
Then the sovereign God Himself
Has surely granted you a child.
A hero full-grown—a son—
Oh, my dear, He has clearly granted you one.
That Koshoy gave his blessing
Means he blessed the child as well.
Dark gray, a hero in his purest form,
Dark-flanked and blue-gray without,
He will have a noble bearing,
And a mane flowing down his back.
His hand will be fierce and open against the foe,
And when he sets out, his road will lie open.
He will subdue whoever he confronts;
His valor will be beyond compare,
A peerless champion, a foremost eagle.
You will have a gray-wolf son,
And you will name him Kenen.
